title: The Disappear by Erica Schmidt at Audible’s Minetta Lane Theatre #the...
transcript: It's canonically understood that marriage is difficult, as is being an artist. It's only logical, then, that two married artists are a disaster waiting to happen. In The Disappear by Erica Schmidt, film director Ben and novelist Mira are in a pretty soured marriage, which you could say is due to Ben's wandering eye for younger women and his general self-centeredness. Much of the first act is spent illustrating their dynamic, humorously contrasting Ben's floundering and chaotic energy with Mira’s emotional groundedness. Thing really come to a head when a project arises where their artistic paths cross, and their teenage daughter becomes caught in the crossfire. A bit uneven but well-paced and well-acted, this play was quite enjoyable. Miriam Silverman is great as Mira, but I found Hamish Linklater's character work as Ben to be the crown jewel of the production. Ben is relentlessly difficult and egotistical, but Hamish plays him so eccentrically and whimsically that you aren't turned off by the character to the point of being uninvested. One aspect of the play that I found especially intriguing, though a little underdeveloped, is the daughter character and how she develops a strong cause for ecological preservation and environmental purity. It's in stark contrast with or maybe even a rebellion to her parents’ obsession with their work, and in turn, with themselves. Despite its messiness, I thought this play was an effective roast and love letter to creatives and all their earnestness, ambition, fragility, self-aggrandizing, and ego. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
